issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Public Transport' is hard to justify from the rest of the profile. The triggers are auditory/name/voice reminders linked to childhood caregiver abuse, and the negative appraisals are shame/self-blame/meaninglessness. Avoiding public transport suggests a situational safety strategy tied to a specific external environment, but there are no threat, memory, or trigger items indicating transport-related danger, crowding, entrapment, or encounters with abuse reminders in that context. This makes the item clinically difficult to integrate with the rest of the selected profile and with the formulation, where maladaptive strategies are closely linked to triggers and appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more characteristically tied to sexual trauma and is difficult to reconcile as a central appraisal in this profile of childhood physical abuse without any supporting memory, trigger, or threat content suggesting bodily violation themes.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding evaluation of appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers childhood caregiver abuse with auditory/name/voice reminders and self-blame/meaning loss. This strategy is not well supported by the listed triggers or appraisals and feels aimed at a different symptom cluster than the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Adeola has been a plumber for twenty years and has always taken pride in her work, in the quiet satisfaction of solving a puzzle hidden within walls and floors. But lately, the work has become a minefield. The call that finally brought her to therapy came from a potential client named Grace. Upon hearing the name, Adeola felt a cold dread wash over her, and she’d abruptly claimed to be booked for the next six months. It was the same name as the aunt who had raised her after her parents died. The name was inextricably linked to the sound of a key in the lock, the heavy thud of shoes on the floorboards, and the low, sharp hiss of her own name being called. The punishments that followed were always framed as being for her own good, a consequence she had brought upon herself. This early lesson—that she was the cause of her own suffering—had hardened into a core belief. She was certain that the abuse happened because of the sort of person she was: difficult, disobedient, inherently flawed.

This belief shadows her every interaction. At a recent job, the building supervisor had a voice with the same rising inflection as her aunt’s. While he was simply explaining a zoning issue, Adeola heard only judgment and the prelude to an attack. She spent the rest of the day in a state of high alert, her muscles tensed, her focus shattered. She found herself replaying his words for hours afterward, twisting them into proof of his malice, dwelling on what he, and people like him, had done to her throughout her life. It felt to her that people in authority were all cut from the same cloth; they saw the defect in her and sought to control or punish it. To protect herself, she has developed a system. She avoids direct eye contact with foremen, communicates with clients primarily through text, and has turned down lucrative commercial jobs because they would require interacting with inspectors and site managers. Her world, once expanding with professional skill, has been systematically shrinking.

The echoes of the past are not just at work. The clatter of a dropped pan on her own kitchen floor can leave her breathless and disoriented, momentarily back in her aunt's small house. Her husband, David, will find her standing rigid, staring at nothing. He tries to comfort her, but his touch feels like an intrusion. She has come to believe there is something fundamentally wrong with her, a kind of permanent damage that makes genuine connection impossible. She watches David laugh while watching television and feels a profound sense of alienation, as if she is observing a life that can no longer include her. Nothing feels meaningful anymore—not the business she built, not the home she and David share, not the future they had planned. It all feels like a hollow performance.

The decision to seek help came after she walked off a major job because the new foreman’s voice triggered her. The lost contract was significant, but it was the look on David’s face that evening—a mixture of fear and exhaustion—that broke through her numbness. He didn’t understand why she was sabotaging her own career, why she was so distant, why the woman he married seemed to be disappearing. For her part, Adeola could not explain it in a way that made sense, because the shame was too immense. She is terrified that therapy will confirm her deepest fear: that she is irrevocably broken. But as she sits in the waiting room, another, smaller part of her clings to the hope that she might one day be able to stand in her own kitchen and hear a dropped pan as just a sound, and not as a verdict.
